articles.title: A 27-year-old from Melbourne who has been through more than 10 operations started a health charity at 21, and with 800 young volunteers and $500,000 raised he is now Victoria’s Young Australian of the Year
articles.summary: A personal experience with serious illness has inspired a young Australian to build a healthcare initiative that is now reaching communities across
articles.body: A personal experience with serious illness has inspired a young Australian to build a healthcare initiative that is now reaching communities across several countries. Ryan Brigham, 27, has been named Victoria’s 2027 Young Australian of the Year for founding Health in Focus, a charity that has brought together more than 800 young volunteers and raised over $500,000 for healthcare programmes. The announcement was made by the National Australia Day Council on November 12, with ABC News and the Victorian Government also reporting on his recognition. Brigham established Health in Focus (HIF) at the age of 21, driven by the belief that access to basic healthcare information and services should not depend on a person’s circumstances or where they live. The organisation works across Australia and internationally, delivering health initiatives and educational programmes aimed at addressing gaps in healthcare access. Its work has since expanded across Australasia, Southeast Asia and Africa, with thousands of patients, students and community members benefiting from its initiatives.More than 800 young volunteers join the initiativeOne of the defining aspects of Health in Focus is its emphasis on involving young people in community healthcare. Rather than limiting its work to fundraising, the organisation gives volunteers opportunities to participate in planning and delivering programmes that respond to local health needs. With more than 800 volunteers involved, HIF has mobilised over $500,000 for its initiatives. The programmes cover different aspects of healthcare support and education, helping communities access resources that might otherwise be difficult to obtain.In Victoria, one of its key initiatives involves mobile cardiac screening clinics. These clinics provide free heart health assessments, with an emphasis on identifying potential cardiovascular problems early. The initiative is particularly important because cardiovascular disease remains a significant public health concern, and early detection can help people seek medical attention before complications become more serious.Personal health struggles shaped his missionBrigham’s work is closely connected to his own experiences with illness. He has spent years dealing with serious health challenges, repeated hospital admissions and more than 10 operations. These experiences gave him firsthand insight into the difficulties people can face while navigating healthcare systems and reinforced his understanding of why access to medical support matters.His journey also shaped his decision to establish an organisation that could make healthcare information and basic support more accessible to people beyond traditional healthcare settings. At 27, Brigham’s recognition highlights how personal experiences can translate into wider community initiatives, particularly when young people are given opportunities to participate in meaningful social work.Four Victorians recognised in the 2027 awardsBrigham was among four recipients announced at the Victorian ceremony, with the awards recognising contributions across healthcare, research, advocacy and community service. Cherie Dear was named the 2027 Australian of the Year for Victoria for her work raising awareness and funding research into pancreatic cancer through the Dare to Hope initiative.Associate Professor Wenn Lawson received the Senior Australian of the Year award for his contributions to autism research, advocacy and education. Lawson, an autistic researcher and author, has spent decades advancing understanding of autism and neurodivergence. Gavin Hynam, known as Bear, was named Victoria’s Local Hero for his Cars 4 Youth programme. He helps young people in regional communities gain independence by repairing and gifting second-hand cars, while also mentoring learner drivers.The four Victorian recipients will join award winners from Australia’s other states and territories for the national Australian of the Year Awards, scheduled to be announced in Canberra on January 25, 2027.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'DMK supports Constitution': Congress praises ex-ally ahead of special Parliament session
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress on Friday heaped praise on the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) and extended an invitation to the opposition meeting scheduled amid
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress on Friday heaped praise on the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) and extended an invitation to the opposition meeting scheduled amid speculation over the Delimitation Bill to be tabled during Parliament’s Special Session.Speaking to reporters, Congress general secretary KC Venugopal said that the DMK always stands with the Constitution of India and that whoever loves the Constitution cannot support the Delimitation Bill.“We are approaching everybody. The DMK always stands with the Constitution of India. I think whoever loves the Constitution of India cannot support these types of divisive agendas,” Venugopal said.“So we will approach all the opposition parties,” he added.This comes as INDIA bloc and other opposition parties are scheduled to meet at 11:30 am on Saturday to discuss their strategy and decide on the next course of action.Venugopal alleged that the Centre, led by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah, was trying to set a “big trap” for the people of India, claiming that this was the design behind the entire episode."The government of India, PM Modi and HM Shah want to set a big trap against the people of India. That is the design of this entire episode,” he said.“INDIA alliance and opposition parties will have a meeting tomorrow morning at 11:30. We will make the strategy and take a decision tomorrow morning at 11:30 am,” he added.This comes amid speculation over the DMK's possible position on the delimitation proposals and allegations by the ruling TVK that the party could be moving closer to the BJP-led Centre.The DMK has, however, denied any move towards an alliance with the BJP.Earlier in the day, DMK chief MK Stalin reiterated the party's two demands on the proposed delimitation exercise, insisting that Tamil Nadu's existing 7.18 per cent share of Lok Sabha seats must not be reduced under any circumstances."No change in position, no compromise, the DMK will never compromise on Tamil Nadu’s interests; nor will it depart from its principles," the party chief asserted on the Centre's expected delimitation move."The shameless and ungrateful lot who abandoned their principles for positions of power must realise this," he said, apparently hitting out at the Congress party, which joined the TVK alliance and the government led by it after the DMK was defeated in the assembly polls held earlier this year.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Two anonymous California landowners donated conservation rights worth $680,000 to protect 120 acres of redwood forest and endangered salmon habitat
articles.summary: Two anonymous landowners in California have made an unusual contribution to conservation by donating a conservation easement valued at more than $680,000
articles.body: Two anonymous landowners in California have made an unusual contribution to conservation by donating a conservation easement valued at more than $680,000 to permanently protect 120 acres of privately owned forest in the Santa Cruz Mountains. The property, located in the Upper Zayante River watershed near Felton, includes more than 67 acres of redwood forest, along with oak woodlands, Douglas fir trees and other diverse habitats. The donation was made to Sempervirens Fund, California's first land trust, in December 2023 and announced publicly on January 4, 2024. The agreement restricts future development, subdivision and commercial timber harvesting while allowing the owners to continue enjoying the property for low-impact recreational activities. The protected landscape also plays an important role in safeguarding waterways connected to endangered coho salmon habitat.Why two anonymous California landowners gave up $680,000 to protect a redwood forestThe property, known to its owners as Isabel Upani, remains in private ownership under the conservation agreement. Rather than transferring the land itself, the owners donated an easement that permanently limits certain activities that could damage its natural environment.The conservation easement prevents development, subdivision and commercial timber harvesting across the 120-acre property. However, the owners retain access and can continue using the land for activities that have a low environmental impact.The arrangement allows the forest and its surrounding ecosystems to remain protected without requiring the owners to surrender the property. Sempervirens Fund will oversee the conservation commitments and undertake stewardship initiatives to improve the health and resilience of the landscape.According to the organisation, the donated easement was valued at $680,235, a figure also recorded in its financial statements for the financial year ending June 2024.More than 67 acres of redwood forest under protectionThe 120-acre property contains more than 67 acres of redwood forest, consisting predominantly of second-growth trees, alongside dozens of surviving old-growth redwoods.The landscape also includes Douglas fir forests, oak woodlands, mixed hardwood forests, maritime chaparral, chamise scrubland and riparian woodland. These different habitats support a variety of native plant and animal species.The forest's older redwood trees are particularly significant because relatively few original old-growth coastal redwood forests remain. The surviving trees provide important ecological structures and contribute to the region's biodiversity.The property's varied vegetation also creates suitable habitat for several rare species, including the San Francisco dusky-footed woodrat, pileated woodpecker and Santa Cruz black salamander, according to Sempervirens Fund.The organisation said the land contains dozens of remnant old-growth redwoods among the more numerous younger trees.How the protected forest could help endangered salmonBeyond its trees and terrestrial wildlife, the property has an important connection to the region's freshwater ecosystem. Its creek and waterways feed into the San Lorenzo River through the Upper Zayante watershed, an important landscape for the recovery of coho salmon and the conservation of steelhead trout.The Central California Coast population of coho salmon is federally listed as endangered, while Central California Coast steelhead trout are classified as threatened.Healthy redwood forests contribute to the protection of these aquatic habitats in several ways. Their extensive root systems help stabilise soil, reduce erosion and regulate water movement. Their canopies also provide shade, helping maintain cooler conditions in nearby waterways.These natural processes are important for fish that depend on suitable freshwater conditions during different stages of their life cycles.By permanently protecting the surrounding forest and waterways from development and commercial logging, the conservation easement helps safeguard habitat connected to the San Lorenzo River. The area is particularly important for long-term efforts to support endangered coho salmon recovery.A larger conservation effort in the Santa Cruz MountainsThe protection of Isabel Upani also contributes to broader conservation work across the Santa Cruz Mountains.Sempervirens Fund, established in 1900, works to preserve redwood forests, wildlife habitats and watersheds across the region. The organisation has protected more than 36,000 acres of land and directly owns or stewards more than 12,000 acres.Its Winter 2024 newsletter highlighted how the 120-acre property, together with other land owned by the organisation, contributes to a 645-acre conservation and restoration refuge.The organisation has outlined plans to improve the health of the landscape through activities such as reducing wildfire fuel, restoring ponds and managing vegetation. These measures are intended to strengthen the resilience of the forest and its waterways.The anonymous landowners' contribution therefore forms part of a wider effort to protect connected natural habitats, preserve redwood ecosystems and support wildlife across California's Santa Cruz Mountains.You use AI every day. articles.title: Chris Preble rushed into a burning Nebraska camper in June and pulled Judy Erickson to safety, suffering serious burns himself; five months later, he has been selected for an honour at the Nebraska-Iowa football game
articles.summary: Some people are God's favourites, not in the way you expect, but in the way they are meant to be.
articles.body: Some people are God's favourites, not in the way you expect, but in the way they are meant to be. They are not always the ones who are spared from life's cruelties; rather, they are the ones who become the reason someone else finds the courage to step into the middle of them. And perhaps, the greatest blessing is not always being saved, but being given the chance to save someone else.“Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.” - John 15:13Some people carry the light of Christ within them, becoming a quiet grace and a light in someone else's darkest hour. Not every person performs miracles, but in moments when another life hangs in the balance, they choose compassion over fear. Chris Preble was one such person. When he saw Judy Erickson trapped inside a burning camper, he ran towards the flames and brought her to safety, even at the cost of suffering serious burns himself. He may not have thought of himself as doing anything extraordinary that morning, but to the woman whose life he helped save, his actions meant everything.According to a report by the Kearney Hub, Preble was near Harlan County Lake in Nebraska on June 14, 2026, when he noticed a camper engulfed in flames. Inside was Judy Erickson, who needed help escaping the fire. Preble rushed into the burning camper and pulled her to safety, suffering serious burns himself. Five months later, his act of courage would earn him a special honour at the annual Nebraska-Iowa football game.A quiet morning by the lake turned into a fight for survivalJune 14, 2026, had begun as an ordinary morning for Chris Preble and his wife, who were spending time near Harlan County Lake in Nebraska. But the quiet outing soon took an alarming turn when Preble noticed a camper on fire at the Patterson Harbor Campground. Inside was Judy Erickson, who was trapped as the flames spread around her.The fire had started inside the RV while Erickson was preparing breakfast for a family gathering. She had turned the gas stove to a low flame and placed a plastic cutting board over it before stepping away. Soon, thick black smoke began filling the camper. When she tried to escape through the sliding glass door, she burned her hand and could not get it open. With smoke making it difficult to breathe, she began calling for help, fearing she might not make it out.By chance, Preble and his wife were driving their golf cart back from the marina when he took a different turn through the campground. He spotted flames coming from the camper's open door and heard Erickson screaming for help. Without stopping to think, he jumped off the golf cart and ran inside. The smoke was so dense that he could barely see, but he reached out, found Erickson and grabbed her. He managed to drag her towards the exit, even falling with her as they made their way through the flames. Once outside, he laid her on the ground before stopping to roll on the ground as his own clothes and body had caught fire.The rescue came at a terrible cost. Preble suffered burns to his head, back, arm and foot, while Erickson sustained burns and smoke inhalation. Both were taken to hospital for treatment.The rescue came at a cost, but Preble's courage did not go unnoticedWhile Judy Erickson had made it out of the burning camper, Preble was left to face the consequences of the fire himself. He had suffered serious burns across several parts of his body and needed medical attention. What had begun as an ordinary morning had turned into a life-altering experience, one that would leave him with a long road to recovery. Yet, for Erickson, his actions had meant the difference between life and death.The weeks that followed were far from easy. Preble suffered burns to his head, back, arm and foot, including third-degree burns on his arm, and underwent a skin-graft procedure in July. His wife, Chris, helped care for his injuries, changing his bandages and cleaning the wounds twice a day. The treatment was painful, often taking nearly an hour and a half each time, but Preble gradually began to recover. By November, he said he had healed almost completely and had returned to playing golf and working.His act of courage also stayed with the people he had helped. Erickson and her family remained in touch with him, and she was among those who nominated him for the honour. Along with his wife and brother, she wanted his decision to run into the burning camper to be recognised.Preble has now been selected as Nebraska's 2026 citizen hero for the 16th annual Heroes Game between the Nebraska Cornhuskers and the Iowa Hawkeyes. He will be honoured at halftime on November 27 at Kinnick Stadium in Iowa City, where he will receive on-field recognition and have his name inscribed on the Heroes Game trophy.Sometimes, courage does not announce itself; it simply appears when someone else's life depends on it. Chris Preble may have entered that burning camper without knowing what awaited him, but he came out having given Judy Erickson another chance at life. The honour he receives five months later is a reminder that some acts of kindness leave a mark far beyond the moment in which they happen.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Norse Atlantic faces termination of leases for all 12 Boeing 787s as cash-strapped airline seeks emergency funding; flights are suspended, bankruptcy remains a risk and it disputes the lessors’ move
articles.summary: Norse Atlantic Airways faces another setback in its fight to survive, as the companies that lease all 12 of its Boeing 787 Dreamliners sent notices ending
articles.body: Norse Atlantic Airways faces another setback in its fight to survive, as the companies that lease all 12 of its Boeing 787 Dreamliners sent notices ending those leases, leaving the cash-strapped airline at risk of losing its planes while it looks for emergency money. On Friday, 27 November 2026, the Norwegian budget airline confirmed it got notices ending the leases for all 12 jets, and although it is fighting the lessors' move, its money trouble got much worse after it stopped all flights and warned that bankruptcy could follow if it cannot get new cash soon. According to a Reuters report shared through Euronext, Norse Atlantic already called its money situation "critical" on Wednesday, and one day later, it stopped its flights while the board kept looking for a short-term money fix.This latest news casts more doubt over the airline's future flights, with aviation analyst John Strickland telling Reuters that the lease-ending notices looked final and that Norse could not fly again unless it beat the lessors' move. "The company contests the validity of the termination notices," Norse Atlantic said in a statement, while adding that it was still talking to investors about possible short-term funding and warning there was no promise a working deal would happen.Lessors move against entire Dreamliner fleetThe 12 planes at the center of the fight are Boeing 787 Dreamliners leased from two big aircraft finance firms, AerCap Holdings, based in Ireland, and BOC Aviation, based in Singapore. In 2021, Norse Atlantic signed long-term lease deals with both firms as it set up its long-haul flights, first leasing nine Dreamliners from AerCap and six from BOC Aviation before later giving three planes back to AerCap, leaving 12 Boeing 787s all covered by the lease-ending notices shared on Friday. According to Norse Atlantic's latest annual report, the AerCap deals were first meant to run for about 12 years per plane, while the BOC Aviation deals had longer terms of about 16 years.The lease-ending notices could take away the planes that keep the airline running, since Norse Atlantic runs a long-haul business built around the Boeing 787, flying between Europe and places in North America, Asia and other regions. The airline has not said it accepts what the lessors did, so whether the lease endings stand is still in dispute as it fights the notices. Reuters asked BOC Aviation for comment, but the Singapore lessor turned down the request, and AerCap did not reply right away when asked for comment.Bankruptcy warning follows suspension of flightsThe lease fight hits Norse Atlantic at a very hard time after the airline had already warned it could run out of choices without fast money help. In a 25 November statement, the airline said it needed new funding to cover short-term cash needs and keep flying, while also confirming it had looked at several options, including a possible takeover or sale of the company, as well as other deals such as aircraft, crew, maintenance and insurance (ACMI) contracts to supply planes and flight crews to other airlines.A day later, on 26 November, Norse said it had stopped all flights while its board kept talking with possible investors, saying in its statement: "If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy." The statement also confirmed talks with investors about a possible takeover tied to a funding deal, after the airline held an information meeting on 25 November with holders of its 15% senior secured bonds, worth $52 million. Norse said sorry to passengers hit by the flight stop, gave no set date for flying again, and now faces an added hurdle because even if it gets new money, it may find it hard to restart its old flights if it cannot keep or get back its Dreamliners.Shares lose almost all their valueThe cash crisis has also hurt Norse Atlantic's stock price, with Reuters reporting that the airline's shares dropped 45% by 08:37 GMT on Friday, 27 November, bringing its losses for the year to 99.6%. That drop came after another big fall on Wednesday, when the airline said its money situation was critical and Reuters reported that the shares fell 85% by the end of trading that day. The sharp drops show investors worry the airline cannot raise enough cash to keep running and pay what it owes. Norse had already started looking into a possible sale or merger in July 2026 and had also talked with other airlines about leasing out some of its Boeing 787s, while its latest money update did not say how much emergency cash it needed or how long it could last without more money.Rising fuel costs add to airline's problemsNorse Atlantic's money trouble has grown as higher fuel prices and flight disruptions squeeze airlines. According to Reuters, the US-Iran conflict, which started near the end of February 2026, helped cause supply snags and big jumps in European jet fuel prices, which more than doubled in March and stayed up and down, pushing up airline running costs. Fuel price swings hit Norse hard because it does not hedge its jet fuel needs, a practice that lets airlines lock in prices or set up money deals ahead of time to guard against sudden price jumps. The airline had already cut back its flying as fuel costs rose, and The Guardian reported on 26 November that Norse started a cost-cutting plan called Project Falcon to save $50 million, covering cutting about 75 jobs and moving its head office from Norway to cheaper offices in Latvia. The airline's founder and chief executive, Bjørn Tore Larsen, had also left as the company pushed through its overhaul, yet those steps have not stopped the current cash crunch.Passengers and international routes affectedStopping flights has disrupted Norse Atlantic's overseas routes, including flights linking the UK with North America, Asia and Africa. The Guardian reported that hit UK routes included flights from London Gatwick to Orlando, Bangkok and Cape Town, along with a winter route from Manchester to Thailand that was also set to start in December. The airline had built its business on low-cost long-haul trips, using its Boeing 787 Dreamliners to link cities across Europe, North America, Africa and Asia, while also using its planes for charter flights and ACMI deals with other carriers. One deal was with Pakistan International Airlines (PIA), which agreed in October to use two Norse Atlantic Boeing 787-9 jets under an ACMI contract, and after Norse stopped flying, PIA said it would move its UK flights to its own Boeing 777 planes starting 26 November. According to Reuters, the sudden flight stop forced two flights from London and Manchester under that deal to be canceled.Aircraft future remains uncertainRight now, the key question for Norse Atlantic is whether it can get funding while fighting the lease-ending notices from AerCap and BOC Aviation, with aviation analyst John Strickland telling Reuters that the lessors' move looked final and that the airline could not fly again unless it beat the notices. The lessors have not shared public details on what they will do next, and ending the lease deals does not by itself prove all 12 planes have already been taken back. articles.body: The Thanksgiving storm continued to disrupt communities across the United States, leaving widespread power outages, flooding and transport delays in its wake. More than 900,000 homes and businesses were without electricity on Thursday evening, with most outages reported across East Coast states, AP reported citing poweroutage.us.The severe weather also prompted water conservation requests in Maryland, where nearly 2 million customers in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties were asked to limit consumption following intermittent power disruptions. The impact stretched beyond the East Coast, with heavy snowfall affecting parts of the central United States and coastal flooding forcing evacuations in California.The weather also disrupted holiday travel, prompting flight cancellations, road closures and emergency rescues in several communities.Flooding and high winds disrupt East Coast communitiesTorrential rain, strong winds and rising tides caused flooding across parts of the East Coast, including New Jersey and New York. New Jersey declared a state of emergency, while weather advisories were issued across areas stretching from northern Georgia to southern New England.In New York City, emergency responders rescued people trapped in vehicles amid rising floodwaters, Mayor Zohran Mamdani has urged residents to prioritise their safety, saying: “There is no destination worth your safety.”Flooding also affected coastal communities in New Jersey. He compared the situation with Hurricane Sandy, which remains a benchmark for severe flooding in the area.Floodwater carried debris onto roads, while some motorists had to be rescued after driving around barricades and into submerged areas. He said he planned to remain indoors with his family, while some of his friends had experienced flooding inside their homes.Parade postponement and travel disruptions add to holiday woesStrong winds in New York City prompted Macy’s to postpone its annual Thanksgiving Day parade until Saturday over safety concerns surrounding the event’s giant balloons, which could be difficult to control between Manhattan’s skyscrapers.The disruption extended to air and rail travel. articles.title: In 1814, a brewery vat burst and sent a wave of beer through London streets; eight people died in one of history's strangest industrial disasters
articles.summary: Picture a normal Monday afternoon that goes sideways, with streets flooded not with rain or sewage but with thousands of gallons of beer.
articles.body: Picture a normal Monday afternoon that goes sideways, with streets flooded not with rain or sewage but with thousands of gallons of beer. Sounds interesting? On October 17, 1814, the residents of a poor London neighborhood fought a deadly flood of dark porter when an enormous brewery vat ruptured, sending a torrent of beer into their homes and narrow streets. What appeared at first to be an amazing industrial accident was to become one of Britain's oddest tragedies, claiming eight lives and leaving an entire neighborhood in ruins.When disaster came out of a breweryThe event was held at the Horse Shoe Brewery, owned by Meux and Company, in the St Giles district of London, close to Tottenham Court Road. Historic UK says that by 1810 the brewery had installed a huge wooden fermentation vat. The structure was some 22 feet high, bound together with heavy iron hoops, and could hold more than 3,500 barrels of porter, a dark beer somewhat like modern stout.It was an old brewery, turning out huge quantities of porter for the swelling London drinker population. The towering storage vessels were the heart of its operations, but their size also made them a serious hazard when structural elements failed.One October afternoon one of the iron hoops on a large vat snapped. The damage did not, at first, represent an emergency. But the pressure in the huge container built up until the weakened structure eventually gave way.Beer Tsunami triggered by chain reactionAs History explains, brewery clerk George Crick had seen the broken iron hoop earlier that afternoon. Such incidents were not unknown to brewery workers and the damage was not seen as an immediate threat.Then, just about 5.30pm, the huge vat exploded. Things went dramatic and its contents ripped through the surrounding structures, damaging nearby beer containers and beginning additional ruptures.In all, the force sent some 320,000 gallons of fermenting porter gushing from the brewery. The pressure blew out part of the brick wall of the brewery, sending the liquid gushing into the surrounding streets, the Historic UK report adds.St Giles Rookery, with its dense population, was especially vulnerable. Its narrow streets and crowded tenements and shabbily kept buildings afforded little shelter from the sudden deluge.Within minutes a torrent of beer and debris rushed down George Street and New Street flooding basement apartments and inundating nearby houses.Eight lives lost in the deadly floodIt was an extraordinary incident and the human toll was deeply tragic. One of the worst hit properties was a house where Mary Banfield and her four-year-old daughter Hannah were having tea. Their home was swept away in a sudden flood and both were killed, says Historic UK.In the next room, an Irish family was having a wake for a two-year-old boy who had died. The collapsing structure and the rushing beer trapped the mourners inside, killing five people, including the child’s mother, Anne Saville. It was the collapse of the brewery wall which killed teenage worker Eleanor Cooper near the Tavistock Arms public house.The history books tell us that the destruction was most severe on the women and children who lived in the neighbourhood’s crowded and vulnerable housing.Rescuers waded waist-deep in beer, broken timber and fallen masonry searching for survivors. Three brewery employees were rescued and another person was pulled alive out of the rubble.A curious aftermath. A controversial verdict.The disaster also brought disturbing scenes once the flooding receded. Historic records from the UK say people gathered up the spilled beer in containers and others were reported to have drunk it straight off the floor. The smell of fermenting beer hung about the neighborhood for months.An inquiry was held after the tragedy, but the brewery was not held legally responsible. The incident was eventually ruled an Act of God, meaning the deaths were accidental and not the result of an offense.History has it that the brewery got parliamentary relief from the excise duties paid on the lost beer, saving them an even bigger financial whack.A moment that changed the way we brewEventually the Horse Shoe Brewery disappeared, the premises being demolished in 1922. Part of the site of the former building is now the London Dominion Theater.But the disaster of 1814 was to have a lasting effect on brewing history. The extraordinary failure demonstrated the perils of large wooden fermentation vessels and helped spur the gradual transition to more robust lined concrete storage tanks.More than two centuries later, London’s Beer Flood is a sobering reminder that even an everyday industrial product can become a deadly force when engineering and safety fail.Image Courtesy: Google Gemini and istockYou use AI every day. articles.title: UK net migration falls below 100,000 as new figures reveal a dramatic shift in the country's post-Brexit migration pattern
articles.summary: Discover the dramatic drop in the UK's net migration figures post-Brexit, revealing a substantial shift from previous trends and the impact of tightened immigration rules.
articles.body: The UK's migration has undergone a significant transformation over the past three decades, with the latest official figures pointing to a sharp reversal in the trend of people moving to the country. Net migration stood at 77,000 in the year ending June 2026, its lowest level outside the Covid-19 pandemic since 1997, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).The latest figure marks a substantial change from the period when overseas arrivals consistently outnumbered departures from Britain. It also follows a sharp rise in immigration during the early 2020s, largely driven by non-EU nationals arriving on work and study visas under the post-Brexit immigration system.Data released by the ONS on Thursday showed that 77,000 more people arrived in the UK and stayed for at least 12 months than left the country during the 12 months to June. This compares with net migration of nearly one million at its peak three years ago.How Britain's migration pattern changed after the 1990sThe balance between immigration and emigration has shifted considerably over the decades. During much of the 1960s and 1970s, more people left Britain than moved to the country, according to historical migration data.That pattern began changing around 1993, when the European Union relaxed its immigration rules. The trend strengthened after several eastern European countries joined the bloc in the mid-2000s, making it easier for their citizens to move to the UK.For several years, the number of people arriving exceeded those leaving, establishing net migration as a consistent feature of Britain's population growth.However, the latest figures reflect a different phase. While emigration has increased gradually in recent years, the more pronounced movement has been in immigration, which rose sharply during the 2020s before declining. The two trends have closely tracked each other, with changes in the number of arrivals having a major influence on overall net migration.Why non-EU migration surged after BrexitThe introduction of a new immigration system in 2021, following Brexit, changed the composition of people arriving in Britain. A significant increase in non-EU nationals entering on work and study visas became a major factor behind the rise in migration.Many of these migrants also brought family members with them, adding to the overall numbers. The increase was accompanied by arrivals through special visa routes introduced in response to humanitarian crises.One such route was created for people leaving Hong Kong after China imposed a national security law in 2021, following protests and unrest. Another provided a pathway for Ukrainians fleeing Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.The surge in arrivals during this period was dubbed the "Boriswave" by critics, referring to the sharp increase in migration under the post-Brexit immigration system introduced during Boris Johnson's premiership.Tighter visa rules contribute to the recent declineThe increase in migration prompted successive Conservative and Labour governments to tighten legal immigration rules. Measures included raising minimum salary thresholds for certain work visas, restricting the types of jobs eligible for sponsorship and limiting the ability of some migrant workers and international students to bring family members to Britain.These restrictions have coincided with a decline in immigration, bringing net migration down from its 2023 peak to 77,000 in the latest reporting period.You use AI every day. articles.title: A whisky bottle went down with the SS Politician in 1941; a diver recovered it 46 years later, and it later sold at auction for £9,200
articles.summary: Discover the fascinating story of a whisky bottle that spent 46 years underwater after the SS Politician shipwreck, its recovery by diver George Currie, and its subsequent auction for £9,200, bringing historical maritime drama to life.
articles.body: According to the Scottish Maritime Museum, a bottle of whisky spent 46 years underwater after the SS Politician ran aground off Scotland in 1941. Diver George Currie recovered it in June 1987 and more than three decades later the Scottish Maritime Museum won it as part of an auction lot for £9,200, the Press and Journal reported. The collection also included Currie's diving helmet and other objects recovered from the wreck. The SS Politician was a cargo ship built in 1923. According to the Scottish Maritime Museum, it left Liverpool on February 3, 1941, bound for Kingston, Jamaica and New Orleans, carrying cars, bicycles, cotton, medicines, tobacco and around £145,000 in Jamaican banknotes. The vessel also had on board a considerable amount of whisky, which was going to play a significant role in Scottish history. According to the Scottish Maritime Museum, Hold No.5 contained 22,000 cases, or 264,000 bottles of malt whisky from bonded warehouses in Leith and Glasgow.How the SS Politician became a famous shipwreckIt was sailing towards a convoy destined for America, but due to severe weather it became necessary for Captain Beaconsfield Worthington to alter its route. According to the Scottish Maritime Museum, the ship hit submerged sandbanks off Rosinish Point on the Isle of Eriskay in the Outer Hebrides at 7:45 a.m. on February 5, two days after leaving Liverpool. There was water seeping inside the ship and the people of the island assisted in rescuing the crew members. The ship became a source of attraction for the locals due to the precious cargo of whisky it was carrying. Locals started retrieving bottles from the stranded ship because they believed the salvage rules gave them a right to the cargo, according to the Scottish Maritime Museum. Customs officers saw it differently, since duty had not been paid on the whisky.Authorities investigated the raids and the Scottish Maritime Museum says some islanders were tried for illegal salvaging, smuggling and black market selling and sentenced to up to six weeks in prison. Customs officer Charles McColl later applied successfully for permission to scuttle the hull to stop any further salvaging, the museum said. The incident inspired Scottish author Compton Mackenzie's 1947 novel Whisky Galore! The Scottish Maritime Museum notes that the story became an Ealing comedy two years later and was remade in 2016. The fictional ship in the novel was named the SS Cabinet Minister.A diver recovered a bottle decades laterAlthough some of the whisky was recovered or lost, other bottles stayed under the water. In June 1987, North Sea diver George Currie and his colleagues went looking for the wreck after finishing a subsea cable repair between South Uist and Eriskay, according to the Scottish Maritime Museum. George Currie found the bottle, which had been submerged underwater for 46 years. Though the original label on the bottle was no longer there, the bottle itself was in good condition and intact. The museum said the production details of the bottle suggest the whisky came from a distillery owned by W & A Gilbey. However, the whisky is now considered unfit for consumption due to the time it spent in the water.Museum acquires the auction lot for £9,200Currie's bottle was sold through The Grand Whisky Auction in September 2020, The Courier reported. The Scottish Maritime Museum won the lot with a £9,200 bid and the lot also included Currie's diving helmet, two bricks from the ship and a poster from the 2016 remake of Whisky Galore! The museum acquired the lot with the support of Scotland's National Fund for Acquisitions, according to its own announcement. The Scottish Maritime Museum planned to use the items to narrate the story of the shipwreck and its recovery, along with smuggling in the Scottish islands. The bottle's value lay not in the whisky itself, which could no longer be drunk, but in its link to the wreck of the SS Politician. This whisky bottle was under the sea for decades.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Pennsylvania widow lived in the same house for more than 45 years after buying it with her husband for $6,000; when his children from an earlier marriage claimed a share, a November 25 court ruled in her favour
articles.summary: A Pennsylvania widow has won a court fight to keep the home she shared with her husband for over 45 years, after her husband's two children from an
articles.body: A Pennsylvania widow has won a court fight to keep the home she shared with her husband for over 45 years, after her husband's two children from an earlier marriage had claimed a share of the house after he died. On 25 November 2026, the Pennsylvania Superior Court backed a lower court ruling for her, finding the couple owned the house together even though only her husband's name was on the deed, so the home belongs solely to the widow, Jane L. Shellhammer, and is not part of her late husband's estate. The fight centered on a house at 776 Edgemont Avenue in Palmerton, Carbon County, which the couple bought in September 1979 for $6,000, where Jane Shellhammer has lived for more than 45 years and paid the bills, upkeep, repairs, upgrades and property taxes on her own after her husband died. In its ruling, the Superior Court said the proof backed the finding that the pair held the home as tenants by the entirety, a form of joint ownership Pennsylvania lets married couples use where full ownership moves straight to the surviving spouse when one spouse dies. The court turned down an appeal by Harold T. Shellhammer, who was a son and the administrator of his father's estate, and his sister, Teresa T. Trudich, while legal site Justia published the full ruling.How the couple bought the houseJane Shellhammer married Harold Lloyd Shellhammer in 1978, and he had two children from an earlier marriage. Right after the wedding, she moved into 776 Edgemont Avenue, which belonged to Harold's mother, May Irene Shellhammer, before leaving about four months later after personal clashes with her mother-in-law and sister-in-law, according to the court record. She rented a place in a nearby town and later bought another house with her husband farther down the same street, while Harold stayed with his mother and visited his wife often at both homes.May Irene Shellhammer died on 15 July 1979, and her will let her son buy the Edgemont Avenue house, along with its furniture, contents and appliances, for $6,000, which the couple paid using money from their joint account at Citizens Bank and Trust Company in Palmerton. They finished the buy on 7 September 1979, yet the deed listed only Harold Shellhammer as owner, and Jane told the court she had never seen the deed until she got a letter from the children's lawyer shortly before the lawsuit started. The court record also noted that Harold had little schooling and could not read or write, while Jane said he told her after the buy that the house belonged to both of them, and their granddaughter, Kerri Ahner, who lived with them for long stretches, also remembered Harold saying the couple owned the home together.Children challenged the widow's ownershipHarold died without a will on 11 March 2002, and after his death, Jane stayed in the house and covered its costs, with the court finding she paid the utility bills, upkeep costs, repair bills, upgrade costs and property taxes herself. Neither of Harold's children paid toward the home's care or costs while their father was alive or after he died, according to the court record.The legal fight started in December 2022 when Harold T. Shellhammer, acting for himself and as administrator of his father's estate, and Teresa T. Trudich filed a case to divide the property, arguing the house should be counted as part of their father's estate. In January 2023, they filed a second case to settle legal ownership of the house, and the two cases were joined for trial in May 2023. A judge held a non-jury trial on 19 April 2024, and on 31 December 2024, the Carbon County Court of Common Pleas ruled for Jane, finding she owned the house and throwing out the children's request to divide it; the children tried to overturn that ruling, but their post-trial request failed on 30 December 2025, and judgment was officially entered for Jane on 8 January 2026.Why the appeal court backed herThe children took the case to the Pennsylvania Superior Court, arguing state inheritance law gave them a share of their father's property under Section 2102 of the Probate, Estates and Fiduciary Code, which gives a surviving spouse half of an estate when someone dies without a will and leaves children who are not also the surviving spouse's children. They also fought the lower court's finding that their father and stepmother held the house together as tenants by the entirety. The appeals court looked at both points, noting that Pennsylvania law usually treats property held by a married couple as a tenancy by the entirety unless clear and convincing proof shows the couple did not mean to own it together, and said this ownership form calls for a valid marriage and four rules covering timing of ownership, title, possession and shared interest in the property.In Jane's case, the judges found the evidence backed the lower court's ruling because the pair were married when they bought the house and the $6,000 came from a bank account they held jointly as husband and wife. Even though only Harold's name was on the deed, the house was their family home for decades, and the court also weighed Harold's remarks to Jane and their granddaughter that both spouses owned the property, noted Jane had lived in the home for 45 years by the time of the trial, pointed to proof that she and Harold split upkeep costs while married and Jane paid them alone after he died, and noted Jane testified the children never told her she did not own the home, offered to help pay its costs, or told her to move out before the court fight began.Inheritance law did not change the outcomeThe Superior Court agreed with the lower court that the inheritance law cited by the children did not decide ownership here, since holding the house as tenants by the entirety meant Jane became its sole owner right away when Harold died. The judges explained that a surviving spouse does not inherit a new share in that setup, because ownership stays with the surviving spouse under the joint ownership already in place, so the house did not go into Harold's estate to be split under intestacy rules. Seeing no reason to overturn the lower court's findings or how it weighed the proof, the court upheld the 8 January 2026 judgment for Jane on 25 November 2026, which also made a separate request by the children, filed on 3 August 2026 to submit another appeal brief, pointless and led the court to dismiss that request as moot. The decision leaves Jane Shellhammer as sole owner of the Palmerton home she has lived in for over four decades.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Odisha saw 17,250 college dropouts in 3 years as 79,961 seats stayed vacant in 2025-26; Ganjam led dropouts; govt rolls out Gyanodaya scheme.
articles.body: Bhubaneswar: As many as 17,250 students discontinued college in Odisha over the past three academic sessions, while higher education institutions in the state had nearly 80,000 vacant seats in 2025-26, according to higher education minister Suryabanshi Suraj. He was replying to MLA Kadraka Appala Swamy in the assembly on Friday.District-wise data show that 5,389 students discontinued courses in 2023-24. The number rose to 6,402 in 2024-25, an increase of about 19% in a year, before declining to 5,459 in 2025-26. Though the latest figure is 14.7% lower than the previous year’s count, it remains slightly higher than the 2023-24 level.Ganjam saw the maximum college dropouts, with a total of 2,095 students discontinuing their courses over 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26, the highest in the state. In 2025-26, Ganjam saw 646 dropouts, followed by Mayurbhanj (538), Balasore (409), Sundargarh (369) and Keonjhar (339). Together, these five districts accounted for 2,301 such students, or about 42% of Odisha’s total for the year.Though the minister did not give reasons, official sources said the students left the courses midway due to poverty and migration to other cities in search of jobs.To increase student enrolment, make higher education more accessible and inclusive, and ensure that no eligible student is deprived due to financial constraints, the minister said the state govt has formulated the ‘Gyanodaya-Shiksharu Samruddhi' scheme.“Under this scheme, fees related to enrolment and re-enrolment for eligible students have been waived. As a result, along with an increase in students’ interest in higher education, an increase in enrolment has also been observed,” he said.Suraj added the state govt is continuously taking steps to expand higher education opportunities and improve its quality.The figures assume significance against the backdrop of a large number of seats lying vacant across higher education institutions. A total of 79,961 seats remained vacant in 2025-26, up from 73,020 in 2024-25, though lower than 85,535 vacancies in 2023-24.The latest vacancy marks an increase of 6,941 seats, or 9.5%, over the previous year. However, compared with 2023-24, vacancies were lower by 5,574 seats, or 6.5%.Non-govt aided colleges under the 488 category accounted for the largest share of vacancies in 2025-26, with 29,727 seats remaining unfilled. Unaided or self-financing colleges followed with 26,863 vacant seats, while non-govt-aided colleges under the 662 category had 19,481 vacancies. Govt colleges had 3,890 vacant seats.The data show a divergence between govt and private institutions. Vacancies in govt colleges declined from 6,819 in 2023-24 to 5,731 in 2024-25 and 3,890 in 2025-26. articles.title: New York state Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins dies at 76
articles.summary: New York state Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins, who shattered the glass ceiling in New York politics by being the first woman to hold this role, has died, Gov.
articles.body: New York state Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins, who shattered the glass ceiling in New York politics by being the first woman to hold this role, has died, Gov. Kathy Hochul confirmed Friday. She was 76 years old. Additional information was not immediately available. Stewart-Cousins was a powerful figure in state politics. She was president pro tempore and majority leader of the New York state Senate while serving as senator for the 35th District. Stewart-Cousins was the longest-serving Democratic majority leader in New York state Senate history, and the first woman and African American woman in the role. In a statement Friday, Hochul called Stewart-Cousins a dear friend. “I’ll never forget the honor of introducing Andrea as Majority Leader for the first time in 2019. I knew how hard she had worked to get there and how many women had dreamed of seeing that day. Andrea made history that day, and every day that followed, she made that history mean something,” Hochul wrote. “Andrea possessed a rare combination of quiet grace and extraordinary strength. She never forgot where she came from, who she was fighting for or the doors she could open for those coming behind her.” Stewart-Cousins, of Yonkers, served in the State Senate since 2007 after being elected the year prior. She was born and raised in New York and started in public service as a Westchester County legislator. She was also the first African American director of community affairs for the city of Yonkers. News of her death shocked the local and state political landscape. In a statement, New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin said she was “heartbroken,” calling Stewart-Cousins a “true trailblazer and a tireless champion for working families.” Westchester County Executive Ken Jenkins said he was “deeply saddened by the sudden passing of my colleague, my mentor, and my friend.” “Andrea was more than just a remarkable public servant; she was a trailblazer, a dedicated advocate for the people of our County, and a leader whose impact will continue to be felt for generations. Her incredible journey through public service, from the Westchester County Board of Legislators to the highest levels of leadership in New York State, reflected her unwavering commitment to making government work for all people,” Jenkins’ statement continued. “Andrea made history, breaking barriers and opening doors for women and people of color, while never lost sight of the communities and the families she represented. Andrea understood that leadership was about more than just holding a title — it was about showing up, listening, building relationships and delivering meaningful results for the people who put their faith and trust in you.” The New York Republican Party also released a statement on the senator’s death, which read: “The NYGOP extends our deepest condolences to the family, friends and colleagues of Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins following her sudden passing. A longtime public servant and trailblazer in New York politics, she leaves behind a significant legacy of service. May she rest in peace.”

articles.title: Seattle bar owner refuses to back down after declaring 'Ladies' Night' is for 'biological women' only
articles.summary: Art Marble 21 owner Danny Pentin stands by his Ladies' Night discount policy as the Seattle Office for Civil Rights reviews two complaints over the email.
articles.body: A Seattle bar owner is standing by his beliefs about biological sex after a leaked email outlining who should receive Ladies' Night discounts ignited controversy — insisting his establishment welcomes transgender customers and has never discriminated against anyone. "Ladies night is for women. Biological women," Danny Pentin, owner of Art Marble 21, said in an email shared with FOX 13. The local Seattle outlet reported that the email also stated that, "Men dressed in women's clothing are not women, nor are they ladies," and also included that, "If they have a mustache, or can grow one, the ladies night promo does not apply to them. If they have an Adam's apple, not applicable." SAN FRANCISCO YMCA CHANGES LOCKER ROOM RULES AFTER TRANSGENDER CONTROVERSY: REPORT Pentin also wrote, "There has to be a place in Seattle that defers to common sense and biology before ideology and politics and we are that place." Pentin, however, told FOX 13 that he is not against those who are going through gender confusion. "No, I'm not anti people. I mean, I love everybody for where they're at, right," Pentin said. "If people who go through dealing with body dysmorphia and those things, those are real things that people have to deal with." According to an Instagram statement from Pentin, the controversy began in late August when a bartender was allegedly assaulted by a customer following a dispute over eligibility for a discounted drink during Ladies' Night. MASSACHUSETTS LESBIAN BAR IGNITES FURY AFTER EASING MASK RULES FOR ONE NIGHT A WEEK Pentin said the bar initially had no formal restrictions on who could receive the discounts, leaving those decisions to individual bartenders. Following the alleged incident, he sent an internal email on Sept. 19, speaking to what he described as customers exploiting a promotion intended for women. Pentin said the email remained private until Nov. 17, when a former bartender leaked it publicly, sparking backlash over his views on biological sex and the bar's discount policy. In his public response, Pentin defended his personal beliefs while insisting that Art Marble 21 has never discriminated against customers or prohibited transgender individuals from entering the establishment. NEW HAMPSHIRE WOMAN SAYS PLANET FITNESS CANCELED HER MEMBERSHIP AFTER SHE REPORTED MAN IN LOCKER ROOM He emphasized that the views expressed in the email were his alone and did not necessarily reflect those of his employees. "On its face the leaked email appears to suggest we do not allow trans people into our establishment," Pentin wrote in the Instagram statement. "That is simply not true. If we did not allow trans people into our establishment, it would have been made known long before this email was taken out of context. My personal stance is made known in the email, but it does not reflect the beliefs of the employees that work at Art Marble 21. These are my beliefs and mine alone. We respect each other's beliefs. My staff would not work for me for years if they believed I was a bigot, a racist or any of the other buzz words used to condemn people who think differently than those who have made this into what it has become." He said he respects people's freedom to live according to their own beliefs and expects that respect to be reciprocated. Pentin concluded by reaffirming his convictions and insisting that Art Marble 21 remains a welcoming establishment, saying it has never been discriminatory and never will be. In a statement to Fox News Digital, a spokesperson for the Seattle Office of Civil Rights said that gender and gender identity are protected classes under Seattle’s Public Accommodations Ordinance that prohibits discriminatory practices, and that businesses cannot legally deny a promotional discount based on a customer's sex, gender identity, or gender expression. FEMALE VIRGINIA OFFICER SUES POLICE DEPARTMENT AFTER ALLEGEDLY SHARING LOCKER ROOM WITH BIOLOGICAL MALE The Seattle Office for Civil Rights said they received two complaints regarding Art Marble 21's "Ladies' Night" promotion, one on Nov. 17 and one on Nov.19, and are "following up with the individuals who submitted the complaints to determine if they qualify to file a claim and whether they wish to proceed with that process." articles.title: Ontario’s Doug Ford calls for US-style self-defense laws after violent home invasions
articles.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Friday that Canada should adopt laws that further protect the right to self-defense after a 39-year-old musician was fatally shot during a home invasion Wednesday in Toronto. “Standing up to home invaders shouldn’t be a crime,” Ford wrote on social platform X. “That’s why we’re calling on the federal government…
articles.body:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Friday that Canada should adopt laws that further protect the right to self-defense after a 39-year-old musician was fatally shot during a home invasion Wednesday in Toronto.

“Standing up to home invaders shouldn’t be a crime,” Ford wrote on social platform X . “That’s why we’re calling on the federal government to make common-sense changes that protect people who protect their homes and families from criminals.”

Also on Friday, Ontario Attorney General Doug Downey and Solicitor General Michael Kerzner urged Canadian Attorney General Sean Fraser to “strengthen and clarify the legal protections available to homeowners” who are confronted with a home invasion.

“Recent Toronto police figures show nearly 120 home invasions in the city this year, an increase of 30 percent over the same period last year,” they wrote in a letter to Fraser . “Behind each incident are people whose safety and sense of security have been threatened in the place where they should feel most secure.”

The two asked Fraser, along with Canadian Minister of Public Safety Gary Anandasangaree, to clarify that a homeowner “has no duty to retreat from their home” before they defend themself.

“A family confronted with violence in their own home should have confidence that reasonable actions taken to protect life and prevent injury will receive the full protection of the law,” wrote Downey and Kerzner, members of the Progressive Conservative Party.

Michael Eckert, a 39-year-old pedal steel guitarist, was shot and killed during a home invasion in Toronto’s Casa Loma neighborhood, according to CTV News .

After the shooting, Ford encouraged Canadians to “use anything you can to protect your family.”

“I encourage people to use whatever tool they have to fight back. Not hide, but fight back,” he told reporters on Thursday, according to CBC .

The Ontario premier, also a member of the Progressive Conservative Party, reportedly noted he is a legal gun owner and called for the province to move “right up to the edge” of the so-called castle doctrine.

“Someone comes through my door with a gun and a knife and starts shooting it up, I’ll blow the guy right through the front door. You’ll look like Swiss cheese by the time he’s done,” the CBC quoted him saying.

There are 36 states in the U.S. that follow the “stand your ground” statute, with Florida being the first to enact such a law in 2005, according to Recording Law .

Those laws remove the “duty to retreat,” the legal requirement that a person cannot harm someone in self-defense when they have a safe way to escape, from situations where a person under threat is lawfully present.

articles.title: Millions clean up after massive Thanksgiving storms on East Coast
articles.summary: Atlantic City had its highest tide since Superstorm Sandy.
articles.body:
The East Coast is recovering from the massive Thanksgiving Day storms that flooded streets, toppled trees and left tens of thousands of homes without power.

As of Friday afternoon, nearly half a million households still didn't have power, the majority of which were in Pennsylvania, according to data from utilities.

Winds gusted between 50 and 70 mph from North Carolina to Massachusetts – taking down powerlines, trees and causing damage to property.

Multiple locations in New Jersey and the Chesapeake Bay hit all-time high tide records on Thanksgiving.

Cape May, New Jersey, recorded their highest tide ever at 9.41 feet.

Atlantic City hit a high tide of 8.28 feet, marking the city's highest tide since Superstorm Sandy in 2012.

Farther south, places in eastern Virginia and North Carolina recorded between three and five inches of rainfall between Wednesday and Thursday. Up to nine inches were recorded at Emerald Isle, North Carolina along the Southern Outer Banks.

Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger declared a state of emergency Friday to help with the recovery efforts of the storm.

"State agencies continue to work closely with local governments and utility partners to restore power to impacted Virginians, maintain safe travel conditions, and support our neighbors," she said in a statement.

All wind alerts expired Friday, although some gusty winds will continue into the day before turning lighter this weekend. Minor coastal flooding will be possible Friday in the Northeast.

By Friday afternoon, rain showers will be moving through New England while some snow is possible across the interior Northeast, especially in the higher elevations of the Appalachians, from Pennsylvania to Virginia.

Weather for the rescheduled Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade looks fine for Saturday morning.

Wind gusts up to 20 to 25 mph are still possible, which is below the parade's safety threshold with mostly cloudy skies and temps in the upper 40s to around 50.

On Sunday, a system in the central part of the country will move east and bring a line of heavy rain and thunderstorms across the Midwest.

The rain stretches from the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley into the Deep South on Sunday afternoon with rain reaching Appalachia by the evening hours. This rain reaches the East Coast on Monday.

articles.title: Mayo Clinic has agreed to pay $906,088 in back wages after Minnesota investigated employees working before their shifts to start computers; appointment staff will now get five paid minutes each day just to log in
articles.summary: A few minutes before the official start of a workday can seem insignificant, but when those minutes become a daily requirement, they can add up to a
articles.body: A few minutes before the official start of a workday can seem insignificant, but when those minutes become a daily requirement, they can add up to a substantial amount of unpaid labour. For employees responsible for answering patient calls and scheduling appointments at Mayo Clinic, starting the workday reportedly meant switching on computers, opening required applications and preparing systems before their shifts officially began. Now, an investigation into these practices has resulted in a settlement requiring the healthcare institution to pay more than $906,000 in back wages and change how it compensates affected employees.Investigation uncovers unpaid work before and after shiftsAccording to CBS News, Mayo Clinic has agreed to pay $906,088.88 in back wages to employees working in its Patient Appointment Services Specialist and lead specialist positions. The settlement comes after an investigation by the office of Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison into allegations that workers were doing job duties outside their paid hours.After workers complained about pay to the AG, the probe began. Workers reportedly said they were expected to arrive before their scheduled shifts to boot up computers and log into the applications necessary for their jobs. They also raised concerns about having to complete patient calls after their shifts had officially ended without receiving additional compensation.The issue extended beyond the time spent preparing computers for the day. According to the Post Bulletin, a civil court filing in Ramsey County alleged that Mayo Clinic used time-rounding practices that could leave some patient appointment services employees without payment for all the hours they worked.Mayo Clinic to end time-rounding practicesA key part of the settlement involves changes to the clinic's timekeeping procedures. The Mayo Clinic has stopped rounding clock-in times for the affected specialists due to concerns that employees could miss pay.The agreement also introduces a specific provision for the daily computer start-up process. Under the new arrangement, affected appointment services employees will receive five paid minutes at the beginning of each workday to switch on their computers and log into the required systems.Yahoo News reported that the settlement also requires Mayo Clinic to maintain policy changes introduced during the investigation to ensure employees receive compensation for the time spent performing their assigned duties.These adjustments are intended to ensure that the preparation required to perform a job is recognised as working time rather than treated as an unpaid responsibility.Attorney General stresses employee compensation rightsMinnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison emphasised that state employment laws require businesses to compensate employees for all time spent carrying out duties connected to their jobs.According to CBS News, Ellison said Mayo Clinic cooperated with the investigation and independently introduced changes to its policies to address the compensation concerns.He also highlighted that employers cannot disregard work performed outside officially scheduled shifts simply because those duties involve preparation or administrative tasks. Employees working on company premises or completing responsibilities related to their jobs must be paid for that time.Ellison further encouraged workers who believe they have been underpaid to contact his office, noting that investigations into workplace compensation practices can potentially benefit other employees facing similar problems.Mayo Clinic agrees to settlement despite disagreementMayo Clinic acknowledged the agreement and said it was intended to resolve concerns involving certain timekeeping practices affecting a group of patient appointment services specialists.According to the Post Bulletin, the healthcare organisation maintained that it did not necessarily agree with the position taken by the Attorney General's Office. However, it considered a settlement that directed financial resources towards employees preferable to spending those resources on legal defence.The clinic also reiterated its commitment to ensuring employees are compensated accurately and appropriately. It said its compensation policies and practices undergo regular reviews to remain aligned with applicable requirements and evolving workplace standards.Questions remain about the number of affected employeesAlthough the settlement establishes a financial resolution and introduces changes to timekeeping procedures, some details have not been publicly specified. Neither the Attorney General's announcement nor Mayo Clinic's statement disclosed the exact number of employees covered by the agreement or the period over which the unpaid wages accumulated.As reported by Yahoo News, the settlement represents more than a financial payment, addressing workplace practices that determine whether employees are properly compensated for every part of their working day.Mayo Clinic appointment staff now receive five paid minutes each morning. It also reinforces a broader principle of Minnesota employment law: work required to perform a job should count as paid working time, even when it begins before the official shift.Image Courtesy: Post Bulltein and Google GeminiYou use AI every day. articles.body:
Prince William praised the impact of the Diana Award on Thursday after the charity named for his late mother announced it could no longer meet its financial obligations.

“The Diana Award has recognised and encouraged thousands of young people who are changing the world for the better,” the Prince of Wales told ABC News . “I want to thank everyone whose dedication and hard work helped make that possible over so many years.”

The Diana Award, established in 1999 to honor the late Princess Diana — mother of William and Prince Harry — said Thursday it “has been placed into Administration, after independent advice made clear that the charity can no longer continue to meet its obligations.”

The charity added on its website , “This is not the outcome any of us wanted. We thank everyone who has supported this charity over the years and, above all, the young people whose achievements have always been at the heart of it.

“Their achievements matter, and nothing about today’s decision changes that.”

The Diana Award said Thursday that more than 50,000 young people have received the honor, adding it has worked with “thousands more” via programs to “power the impact created by these inspirational young leaders” on those around them.

The charity’s directors appointed Nick Parsk of Oury Clark Chartered Accountants as joint administrator of the company, it said.

Neither William nor Harry hold an official position at the charity, ABC News reported.

articles.title: What we know about the Princess of Wales’ new documentary
articles.summary: Catherine, Princess of Wales will give an unusually personal insight into life since her cancer diagnosis in a new documentary which follows her healing journey.
articles.body: Catherine, Princess of Wales will give an unusually personal and moving insight into life since her cancer diagnosis in a new documentary which follows her healing journey. In the film, which premieres Sunday on the BBC for British viewers, cameras follow Kate, who revealed she was in remission in January 2025, as she takes on the National Three Peaks Challenge – one of the UK’s toughest mountain endurance tests – while reflecting on her experience along the way. The mom-of-three completed the task in June this year, scaling the highest peaks in Scotland, England and Wales within 24 hours to raise money for the Royal Marsden Cancer Charity, which supports the hospital where she underwent treatment two years ago. “This was an idea I had in the spring, not simply as a physical challenge but as a way of giving back to a community that holds great meaning for me and whose care and expertise are life-changing for so many people,” the 44-year-old princess said at a preview screening earlier this week. In the film, Kate reflects on mortality and healing, meets others affected by cancer and is joined by her brother James, before receiving an emotional surprise from her children. Here are some of the highlights: 1. She had to accept that ‘life is not infinite’ Early in the 30-minute documentary, Kate describes how cancer goes beyond physical changes and forces a person to confront their own vulnerabilities. “When you’re faced with your own mortality, you have to accept that life is not infinite,” she says, adding that the experience opens you up and “softens” your heart. For her, the challenge is a chance to explore what life and healing look like “beyond diagnosis, beyond treatment.” 2. She wasn’t sure she’d be able to finish the challenge Kate says conquering the Three Peaks is “a personal milestone” in her recovery, while also acknowledging that healing itself has no clear finish line. “I don’t know what it’s going to be like. I don’t know if my body is physically strong enough yet,” she admits. “I’ve been training, but I don’t know if it’s enough. But this is really to understand that, you know, healing is a journey.” She compares the challenge to “more of a pilgrimage” as she follows the same paths climbed by others on their own journeys of recovery. Many cancer patients ring a bell to mark the end of treatment and the beginning of a new phase. But Kate never rang one, previously unaware of the tradition. “I didn’t even know it was a thing,” she tells her brother James Middleton as the pair ascend Scafell Pike, England’s highest mountain and war memorial. “Maybe this is your ringing of the bell,” he tells her. “I should’ve brought a bell with us.” 3. Why she loves being outdoors Kate has often spoken of her love of the natural world, hailing how it can support social and emotional wellbeing. She describes it as “my sanctuary and my refuge.” “Even when I physically couldn’t get into nature, I imagined nature from my hospital bed,” she explains. “And now that I’m well enough, I feel a deep longing for all those spaces, for the ocean, for the trees, for the mountains.” For the princess, the call of the wild feels almost spiritual. “I find that sense in nature more than anywhere, this feeling that you are part of something bigger and that something else holds you, even often when you can’t hold yourself.” 4. Kate remembers a hand in the darkness Kate recalls a “really dark” period in hospital when she was in and out of consciousness. What she remembers most is someone holding her hand. “They weren’t talking to me. They weren’t trying to fix anything. They were just there,” she says. “You just need to be there. And that’s what love looks like.” Her time in hospital also changed how she sees everyday life. “Something like cancer strips everything away,” she says. The experience, she says, taught her to slow down and be present in the moments that matter, a lesson she has also carried into parenting. “We spend so much time doing and not being. And it’s a lesson that I’ve taken into being a parent too. Just being next to them, alongside them, is enough.” 5. A surprise from William, George, Charlotte and Louis At the top of the second mountain, Kate’s brother reveals he’s been in cahoots with her husband Prince William for a well-deserved reward, as James turns his phone to reveal video messages from her three children. “Hello, Mummy. I really love you and I hope you do well going up the mountain. Remember, I’m always in your heart with you, and I love you very much,” eight-year-old Prince Louis can be heard saying. Next, her eldest, Prince George, tells her to “keep going” and informs his mom that he’s tracking her and she looks “really strong.” Princess Charlotte adds that the family is “so proud of you doing your walk and your challenges.” Moved by the messages, Kate says, “They gave me the reason to get out of hospital. They’re going to give me the reason to finish this challenge.” And so she does. “Oh my gosh. Well done, body,” she tells herself after reaching the summit of the third and final mountain in Wales. When she gets back to the bottom, Charlotte and Louis are seen leaping into their mom’s arms, a big grin on the princess’ face. She later appears overcome with emotion as she kisses George on the forehead and hugs him tight. Kate says she set out to make a film that she hoped would encourage compassion. Her final message, which extends beyond her own journey, is that “whatever road you face, whatever challenge (lies) ahead, you are not alone. And that beauty and joy can still be found, even amidst the darkest of times.” “Heal” airs in the United States on NBCUniversal on Monday, followed by Channel 9 in Australia on Tuesday and CTV and Noovo in Canada on December 7.
