articles.title: Zohran Mamdani has successful surgery for torn Achilles and will make full recovery, staff says
articles.summary: Surgery to repair New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s Achilles tendon went well Friday and he’s now recovering at Gracie Mansion, his press secretary said.
articles.body: Surgery to repair New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s Achilles tendon went well Friday and he’s now recovering at Gracie Mansion, his press secretary said. “The surgery was successful, and the Mayor is expected to make a full recovery,” the mayor’s press secretary, Joe Calvello, said Friday afternoon. Mamdani underwent the procedure just after 11:30 a.m. and was done about 70 minutes later. “He was discharged from the hospital and is now resting comfortably at Gracie Mansion,” the press secretary said. “We are extremely grateful for the first-class care the Mayor received from the medical staff today.” First Deputy Mayor Dean Fuleihan is leading day-to-day operations today in Mamdani’s stead. The first-term mayor tore his Achilles while playing a friendly soccer game between City Hall and the New York City press corps last week, during which he scored a goal. He showed up to a news conference on Nov. 20 in crutches. “I forgot that I was 35, and soon after, I tore my Achilles,” Mamdani said at the time, noting he didn’t stretch before the game. “I will be in a boot for six to eight weeks. I will play soccer in about nine months.” During a Q&A following a news conference on Monday, the mayor said he admitted he was nervous about the procedure. “I’m scared,” he said. “It’ll be my first surgery.” Due to his recovery, Mamdani will miss the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, which was rescheduled to Saturday.

articles.title: A venomous tiger snake slithered into a Melbourne childcare centre while children prepared for outdoor play; teachers evacuated the room before a professional snake catcher arrived
articles.summary: A routine morning at a childcare centre in Melbourne took an unexpected turn when a highly venomous tiger snake made its way inside the building while
articles.body: A routine morning at a childcare centre in Melbourne took an unexpected turn when a highly venomous tiger snake made its way inside the building while children were getting ready for outdoor play. The reptile was spotted moving through an area used by the young children, prompting educators to move them away and clear the room. With the snake still inside the premises, staff contacted a professional catcher to remove it. Reportedly, Mark Pelley, a local snake catcher known as the Snake Hunter, responded to the call. He later described the incident as one in which a small change in circumstances could have had serious consequences, particularly because young children may not recognise a snakebite or immediately report one.Tiger snake enters childcare centre in Diamond CreekThe incident occurred at a childcare facility in Diamond Creek, in Melbourne's north-east, according to a report by Nine.com.au. The snake entered through an open doorway while the children were preparing for their activities. Pelley said the reptile moved through the area where the children were gathered before approaching the spot where educators were applying sunscreen. The presence of the snake was particularly concerning because the children were close to the ground and might not have noticed it moving nearby.The situation was brought under control by the quick response of one of the educators. Rather than attempting to handle the animal, she directed the children away from it and arranged for everyone to leave the room. Other staff members were informed, allowing the centre to keep the children away from the reptile until professional help arrived.How the snake catcher prepared for the emergencyPelley was contacted while the tiger snake was still inside the childcare centre. He was already dealing with another snake-catching job when the news reached him, but the nature of the call meant he had to prepare for a potentially complicated removal. During the drive to Diamond Creek, he considered how he would approach the animal without causing further alarm. He also had to account for the possibility that a child might have been bitten without anyone noticing.His experience in handling venomous snakes helped him manage the situation. Pelley has been catching snakes since he was seven years old and has worked professionally in the field for more than a decade. He now responds to emergency calls across the area, sometimes attending as many as 15 incidents in a single day. Once inside the centre, his first priority was to secure the tiger snake. He also spoke with the educators, who were understandably concerned about whether any of the children had been bitten.Why identifying a snakebite in young children can be difficultAfter removing the immediate threat, Pelley asked the staff to help establish whether any child could have come into contact with the reptile. He explained that a bite may not always be recognised straight away, particularly in younger children who might struggle to describe what happened. The sensation can be mistaken for an ordinary knock or a strike against the leg, he said. A child might therefore continue playing without realising that a snake has bitten them. He briefed the educators on possible snakebite symptoms and urged them to call Triple Zero (000) immediately if they had any doubts about a potential bite.Snake catcher responds to multiple calls each dayThe Diamond Creek incident is one example of the calls Pelley handles through his snake-catching work. Having started catching snakes as a child, he has spent much of his life learning how to approach and safely remove reptiles from residential and public spaces. articles.title: Russian sabotage spikes in Europe, including ‘risk of mass-casualty incident’: Analysis
articles.summary: Incidents of sabotage blamed on Russia in Europe were up 16 percent year-over-year in September, according to a new report, which warns about the potential for a future “mass-casualty” event by Moscow. The report from the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said the Kremlin’s “unconventional war” on Europe has included attacks on critical infrastructure…
articles.body:
Incidents of sabotage blamed on Russia in Europe were up 16 percent year-over-year in September, according to a new report, which warns about the potential for a future “mass-casualty” event by Moscow.

The report from the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said the Kremlin’s “unconventional war” on Europe has included attacks on critical infrastructure by Russian intelligence services.

“Russian sabotage in Europe has increased even as total recorded activity has fallen,” the report stated. “In the 12 months to September 2026, sabotage incidents rose by 16%. The use of arson and explosives roughly doubled.”

But the campaign has “so far failed in its strategic purpose” to disrupt and undermine support for Ukraine, the IISS analysts added, noting European countries are still supporting Ukrainian militarily and the continent’s defense spending in 2025 outpaced Russia by 9.6 percent.

Russia’s war against Ukraine will hit the five-year mark in February, if it persists until then. Russian attacks in October killed 372 Ukrainian civilians and injured 1,981 civilians, according to the U.N. Human Monitoring Mission in Ukraine .

That marked a 95-percent increase from October 2025, the United Nations reported, adding, “The latest figures show that this year has seen significantly higher casualties than previous years.”

Looking ahead, the IISS projected it is “highly likely” that Russian intelligence will target Germany and Poland the most among European countries. German and Polish transport, logistics and industrial networks are “central to supplying Ukraine,” per the report.

“Sabotage has not yet achieved a strategic effect, but a mass-casualty incident is possible as the space for miscalculation narrows,” the analysts continued, adding that such an incident “would generate demands for retaliation and likely expose divisions” among European governments.

“The effect is that the first mass-casualty attack (deliberate or by miscalculation) would set the terms of Europe’s response, with governments acting under pressure and possibly divided,” the report added.

The analysis comes after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky this week expressed confusion at President Trump recently calling Russian President Vladimir Putin his “friend,” saying it was “strange” considering the ongoing conflict.

Zelensky told BBC , “He can’t be a friend, a friend. Just cannot be. It’s the same that somebody [says] about [Adolf] Hitler during the Second World War that he is a good friend. No, he is not a friend.”

articles.title: Eagles kicker didn't get ex-NFLer's memo about not digging into post-game Thanksgiving food
articles.summary: Derek Carr shares the cold Thanksgiving turkey warning that Eagles hero Jake Elliott apparently missed after his 59-yard field goal beat the Cowboys.
articles.body: Thanksgiving is a day for cramming absurd amounts of food into your mouth hole — and giving thanks, I suppose — but one ex-NFLer has a pro tip about when to show a little restraint. And it would seem that Eagles' Thanksgiving hero Jake Elliott missed the memo. Back in 2021, Derek Carr also led his team — the Las Vegas Raiders at the time — to a Thanksgiving win over the Dallas Cowboys. COWBOYS LEGEND RANDY WHITE REVEALS INTENSE ENCOUNTER BETWEEN HIS MOTHER AND EAGLES FANS DURING PLAYING CAREER As is tradition, he got to help himself to some of the broadcast's Turkey Day grub along with that game's hero, kicker Daniel Carlson. "I have to share this every year," Carr said on his podcast "Home Grown with David & Derek Carr," per Daily Mail. "So we're up there, we do the interview... and obviously Daniel made his kick. We're like: 'Daniel, you're going to eat the turkey.'" Of course, few things top a good Thanksgiving meal, but we usually mean one that came straight out of the oven. "It's definitely cold... [but] he goes to take a bite, and he says: 'Oh, delicious!'" Carr recalled. "And right as we walk away, I said, 'How was it?' He said: 'It was the grossest thing I've ever tasted.'" It makes sense, especially for a game that goes down to the wire, that the food was prepped well in advance. Of course, that also means it's not in its optimal eating window. GIANTS STAR CAM SKATTEBO REVEALS THE ODD PREGAME MEAL THAT CAUSED TO HIM TO PUKE MID-GAME Well, Elliott must not be subscribed to Carr's podcast because after sealing the Eagles' historic 39-38 comeback win with a 59-yard field goal, he dug right in. Hey, the taste of sweet, sweet victory goes nicely with food that was probably intended just to be set dressing. But, lest you think that Elliott had to do his Black Friday shopping while lying on the floor of his bathroom between bouts with food poisoning, think again. The Eagles' hero was right back at it, getting fans fired up before the Philadelphia Flyers' Black Friday game against the Vancouver Canucks. articles.title: Thousands of Puerto Ricans join ‘Day of National Outrage’ protest
articles.summary: Anger and frustration erupt over record-high electricity rates, surging cost of living and deteriorating basic services.
articles.body:
Thousands of Puerto Ricans have protested in the capital, San Juan, as anger and frustration erupted over record-high electricity rates, the surging cost of living, deteriorating basic services and other issues.

Retirees, university students, bus drivers and others joined Friday’s protest organised by some 30 groups ranging from unions to religious organisations. The crowds gathered in front of a mall for what organisers dubbed the “Day of National Outrage”.

Hundreds of demonstrators arrived by bus in San Juan from dozens of cities and towns across the island.

Asked what problems Puerto Rico had, 74-year-old Radames Garcia Badillo said: “Where to start? The outrage is absolute.”

He said that power and water services are unreliable and that his neighbourhood goes dark at least once a week for several hours. He also decried a sharp increase in the cost of living.

“We’re buying less because things are extremely expensive,” he said. “For us retirees, it is essential to make every dollar stretch.”

The protest, one of the largest in the US territory since Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez took office in January 2025, grew throughout the day as demonstrators took over one of the island’s main highways, forcing its closure.

Organisers estimated that some 8,000 people took part, according to local media.

Many in the crowd waved or wore the Puerto Rican flag. Some chose the flag from before the island became a US commonwealth in 1952, often a sign of cultural pride and sometimes of resistance.

“Things have never been good in Puerto Rico, but they keep getting worse,” said Veronica Ishtar, a visual arts student.

This week alone, she said the power in her neighbourhood went out 12 times.

In addition, monthly electricity bills for some residential customers recently rose about 18 percent, with the new rate per kilowatt-hour far surpassing the average for residential customers on the US mainland, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Some protesters blamed Luma Energy, a private company that oversees the transmission and distribution of power on the island.

Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court approved a move to cancel the government’s contract with Luma on Wednesday, but many now worry about what comes next.

Puerto Rico’s Association of Industries said the cancellation could discourage private investment and jeopardise existing projects as crews continue to repair a grid razed by Hurricane Maria in 2017.

The leaders of several groups that organised the protest pledged to keep pushing for change.

“We must begin to channel the rage,” said Hernaliz Vazquez, executive director of Sierra Club Puerto Rico. “We must begin to organise the indignation felt by people who do not know what to do.”

images.caption: Demonstrators march during a protest over high electricity rates, the surging cost of living and deteriorating basic services in San Juan, Puerto Rico, on November 27, 2026 [Alejandro Granadillo/AP]

articles.title: Taiwan votes in local elections to choose mayors, other leaders
articles.summary: Key mayoral race in Taipei, a stronghold of the opposition Kuomintang, tests the governing Democratic Progressive Party.
articles.body:
Taiwan is choosing mayors, council members and other local leaders across its 22 cities and counties in an election that has been unusually competitive in some of the island’s biggest cities.

Polls opened at 8am (00:00 GMT) on Saturday and will close at 4pm (08:00 GMT), with results expected early in the evening.

Voters are casting ballots at schools, temples and community centres.

About 11,000 positions are at stake in the “nine-in-one” elections, named for the nine categories of local government posts being contested.

A key contest is for the mayor of the capital, Taipei, a traditional stronghold of the opposition Kuomintang (KMT).

Mayor Chiang Wan-an of the KMT, who won by a double-digit margin in the last election and is seen as a possible future presidential candidate, faces a strong challenge from Puma Shen of the governing Democratic Progressive Party (DPP).

Shen is an academic-turned-lawmaker and an expert on China’s information warfare . China has denounced him, and Chinese police say he is wanted for “separatism”. He entered the race as the underdog, but has drawn huge crowds at his rallies.

Shen’s victory in the KMT’s heartland could be seen as “quite shameful” in Beijing, said Austin Wang, a political scientist at the University of Nevada.

Chiang told supporters the race was “very close”.

Shen cancelled a final rally over traffic concerns and held an online event instead, which drew more than 500,000 viewers on YouTube. President William Lai Ching-te of the DPP also urged voters at a rally in neighbouring New Taipei City to back the party’s candidates there.

Other notable races are in New Taipei City, Taiwan’s most populous city, and Kaohsiung, in the south. New Taipei City’s incumbent mayor is from the KMT, while Kaohsiung’s mayoral office is held by the DPP.

The vote will not directly change Taiwan’s China policy, and campaigns have focused on local issues such as transport, childcare and the environment.

Beijing, which claims Taiwan as its own territory, has repeatedly weighed in, and the vote is being closely watched there.

Taiwan’s Defence Ministry said it tracked 30 Chinese military aircraft around the island on Friday, 26 of which crossed the median line of the Taiwan Strait in a “joint combat readiness patrol” with warships.

Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council has warned that Beijing is trying to influence the outcome through “cognitive warfare” and “transnational repression”.

China’s Defence Ministry said this week that “reunification” is an unstoppable trend.

In the last local elections four years ago, the KMT won 14 cities and counties, the DPP five and other parties or independents three. The KMT traditionally favours closer ties with Beijing, while the DPP rejects China’s sovereignty claims.

Analysts say local results are an unreliable guide to the outcome of the next presidential election, due in early 2028. Lai is expected to seek a second term.

The KMT could begin debating its presidential ticket soon after the vote. The likely candidates include outgoing Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen and parliamentary speaker Han Kuo-yu.

KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun, who met Chinese President Xi Jinping in April, is also seen as a possible challenger, though she could face pressure to step down if the party does badly.

Kuomintang (KMT) Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an steps forward on stage in front of fellow KMT candidates and speaks during an election-eve campaign rally on November 27, 2026, in Taipei, Taiwan [Cheng Chia Huang/Getty Images]

Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) gives a short speech to supporters during a campaign motorcade ahead of Taiwan’s local elections in Taipei on November 27, 2026 [AFP]

articles.title: Hunted beyond borders: Allegations of Tanzanian repression in Kenya
articles.summary: The case of a missing activist raises fears for the safety of Tanzanian dissidents.
articles.body:
Nairobi, Kenya – On October 25, 2026, Tanzanian opposition activist Twaha Salim Mwaipaya was travelling in a taxi to visit friends in Kamulu, in Kenya’s Machakos County, when three vehicles intercepted it.

According to the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR), unidentified individuals forcibly removed him from the taxi and took him away. His whereabouts remain unknown.

Amnesty International reported that the vehicles included a Toyota Land Cruiser Hardtop. The organisation called on Kenyan authorities to establish Mwaipaya’s whereabouts, guarantee his safety and investigate the circumstances of his disappearance.

The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT) subsequently described the incident as an enforced disappearance and called for an independent investigation, including into possible cross-border involvement.

The identities of those responsible have not been established, and it remains unclear who ordered the abduction.

Mwaipaya, a former youth organiser of Tanzania’s opposition party Chadema, had fled to Kenya in 2025, citing threats to his safety.

On November 3, Kenya’s inspector general of police, Douglas Kanja, appeared before the High Court to explain the activist’s whereabouts. He denied that Kenyan police had arrested or detained Mwaipaya.

“We do not have him in our custody,” Kanja told the court, adding that investigations were ongoing. He acknowledged that Mwaipaya’s relatives had reported him missing at a police station in the Ruai area.

Kanja also said he had consulted other security agencies but had received no information confirming that Mwaipaya had been transferred to Tanzania.

The case returned to the High Court on November 23. Judge Alexander Muteti summoned Mohamed Amin, head of the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI), to provide an update on the investigation into Mwaipaya’s disappearance.

The judge said Amin’s appearance was necessary because the inspector general had placed the investigation within the DCI’s mandate. The court declined to summon Deputy Inspector General of Police Eliud Lagat, ruling that his testimony would not add significant value to the proceedings. Amin was ordered to appear on a date to be determined by the court.

Tanzania’s high commissioner to Kenya, Bernard Kibesse, told news outlet The Citizen on October 26 that the embassy was following up on the disappearance but had not received an official report.

Mwaipaya’s disappearance recalls the January 2025 abduction of Tanzanian activist and government critic Maria Sarungi Tsehai in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi. Unidentified men forced her into a vehicle before releasing her several hours later following public pressure and intervention by human rights defenders, according to reports at the time by Amnesty International Kenya and other organisations.

Sarungi believes her abductors intended to take her across the border into Tanzania.

“In 60-90 minutes, they would have reached the border and crossed with me, and I would have disappeared for good like hundreds of Tanzanians who have disappeared in such manner in Tanzania under Samia Suluhu,” she told Al Jazeera.

She said some of the men appeared to be Kenyan, while another appeared Tanzanian based on his Kiswahili. She alleged that a Tanzanian national directed the operation. The identities of her abductors and who organised the operation have not been independently established.

The incidents have renewed concerns about the safety of Tanzanian dissidents in Kenya and allegations of transnational repression.

In May 2026, President Samia Suluhu Hassan made remarks about dealing with antigovernment protesters that drew criticism.

Speaking alongside Kenyan President William Ruto at State House in Dar es Salaam on May 4, Hassan said protesters should be flogged with canes if they crossed into either country, The Standard reported.

The leaders were attending a joint press briefing following the signing of eight bilateral agreements.

“I have told President William Ruto we must stand firm against those who lack discipline. We should not choose between Tanzanians or Kenyans. If they come to me, I flog them with canes; if they come to you, you flog them with canes, so that they behave,” Hassan said, according to The Standard’s May 5 report.

Former Kenyan Chief Justice David Maraga condemned the comments, describing them as abhorrent. No evidence has emerged linking the remarks to either abduction.

Political repression in Tanzania predates Hassan’s presidency. Under her predecessor, John Magufuli, human rights organisations documented restrictions on political freedoms, intimidation of opposition figures and attacks on government critics.

In September 2017, opposition leader Tundu Lissu survived an assassination attempt in Dodoma, the capital of Tanzania, during which he was shot 16 times by unidentified men. He received treatment in Nairobi before continuing his recovery in Belgium. The attack remains unresolved.

Hassan initially raised hopes of political reform after taking office in 2021, easing restrictions on political rallies and allowing some politicians who had fled the country to return.

However, human rights organisations subsequently documented renewed restrictions on opposition activity, arbitrary arrests and intimidation of critics. The African Union’s 2025 election observation mission also noted that the political opening following her accession had been short-lived.

Lissu was arrested in April 2025 and charged with treason. On November 6, 2026, a Tanzanian court acquitted him of treason but convicted him of incitement, sentencing him to four years in prison.

The Reuters news agency reported that the charges arose from remarks prosecutors said urged supporters to disrupt the election. Lissu denied wrongdoing.

The treatment of critics has also affected activists from neighbouring countries.

In May 2025, Kenyan activist Boniface Mwangi and Ugandan human rights defender Agather Atuhaire travelled to Dar-es-Salaam to observe Lissu’s treason proceedings. They were arrested on May 19 and subsequently deported.

Both later described being held incommunicado and subjected to abuse. Amnesty International reported allegations of torture and ill-treatment, including sexual violence, while United Nations human rights experts issued a communication to the Tanzanian government detailing allegations of enforced disappearance, torture and other abuses. These were allegations documented by the organisations and UN experts, not judicial findings.

Tanzania’s political crisis intensified following the October 29, 2025 general election, which was marked by restrictions on opposition participation and deadly post-election violence.

The African Union Election Observation Mission concluded that the elections did not comply with AU democratic principles and international standards. It cited restrictions on political competition, shortcomings in the electoral framework and an internet shutdown that disrupted observation.

The disputed vote triggered protests, arrests and a security crackdown. Human Rights Watch reported that police and people in civilian clothing killed hundreds of protesters and bystanders.

A year later, the organisation said authorities had yet to make arrests for human rights violations committed before and during the election.

A presidential Commission of Inquiry reported that 518 people died from unnatural causes during the unrest. Its chairman, retired Chief Justice Mohamed Chande Othman, said the figure might not be conclusive.

The commission also recorded allegations that security officers shot people in their homes and shops. Human Rights Watch criticised the inquiry for failing to meaningfully scrutinise the conduct of security forces.

The figures remain contested. Chadema and other sources have reported higher death tolls, although these estimates have not been independently established.

A CNN investigation published on November 20, 2025, analysed geolocated videos, audio evidence and witness accounts showing police and armed men shooting at protesters, including some who appeared unarmed.

It also documented evidence supporting witness accounts of overflowing morgues and possible mass graves. The Tanzanian government disputed aspects of the reporting.

Mwaipaya’s disappearance raises questions about Kenya’s responsibility to protect foreign nationals within its territory, particularly those fleeing political persecution.

Kenya has long provided refuge to activists and opposition figures escaping repression elsewhere in the region. However, the cases of Mwaipaya and Sarungi have raised concerns about whether that protection can be guaranteed when critics of neighbouring governments are allegedly targeted on Kenyan soil.

The Kenyan authorities must establish Mwaipaya’s whereabouts, investigate the circumstances of his disappearance and identify those responsible. Tanzania, meanwhile, must address allegations that its critics are being pursued beyond its borders.

For Tanzanian human rights lawyer Tito Magoti, the disappearances are part of a wider human rights crisis facing the country.

“Tanzanians are not free. Abduction is one side of the coin. There are plenty of other atrocities committed against Tanzanians and they run hand in hand with the abductions. It starts there. You abduct, you torture, you extrajudicially kill, persecute through judicial forums, sexual assault and more, so the state of political freedom is in limbo,” he said.

images.caption: The abduction of Tanzanian opposition activist Twaha Salim Mwaipaya in Kenya has renewed concerns over the safety of government critics fleeing political repression [File: Ben Curtis/AP Photo]
